title: Accrual vs cash basis, and depreciation
summary: Two ways to time revenue and expenses with the custom bike build example, then straight-line depreciation and the delivery van's five-year schedule.

chunks.heading: Cash basis vs accrual basis
chunks.explanation_md:
**The difference is timing:** when do you record revenue and expenses?

**Cash basis**
- Record revenue **when cash is received** and expenses **when cash is paid**.
- **Simple**; used by **small businesses and freelancers**.

**Accrual basis**
- Record revenue **when earned** and expenses **when incurred**, **regardless of when cash moves**.
- **Required under GAAP for most companies**; it **matches revenue to the period it was earned**.

The closing slide's version: **accrual accounting times revenue and expenses to when they occur.**

key_terms.meaning: Record revenue when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid.
Record revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash moves.

chunks.exam_line: Cash basis follows the cash; accrual basis records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, and is required under GAAP for most companies.

chunks.heading: Worked example: the custom bike build
chunks.explanation_md:
**Northstar Bike Co. completes a custom bike build on December 28, 2025 and invoices the client $2,000. The client pays on January 15, 2026.**

| | Cash basis | Accrual basis |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue recorded in... | **January 2026** (when paid) | **December 2025** (when earned) |

The work was finished in December, so under accrual the $2,000 belongs to December 2025. Cash basis waits for the money, so it lands in January 2026.

This is the GAAP principle of **revenue recognition** in action: **recognize revenue when it's earned, not necessarily when cash is received.**

**Exam trap from the quick check:** under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when it is **earned, regardless of cash timing**. Not when it is invoiced, not when it is received in cash, and not when it is approved at year-end.
chunks.exam_line: Custom bike build: cash basis records the $2,000 in January 2026 (when paid); accrual basis records it in December 2025 (when earned).

chunks.heading: Depreciation and the straight-line formula
chunks.explanation_md:
**Depreciation** means **spreading the cost of a long-term asset over the years it's used, instead of expensing it all at once.**

**Straight-line formula:**

**Annual Depreciation = (Cost - Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life**

**Example: Northstar Bike Co.'s delivery van**
- Cost: **$32,000**
- Salvage value: **$2,000**
- Useful life: **5 years**

($32,000 - $2,000) ÷ 5 = **$6,000 per year**

So instead of one $32,000 expense in year 1, the van is expensed at $6,000 a year for 5 years. Notice the formula subtracts the salvage value first, then divides by the useful life.

The quick check asks how depreciation expense is best described: **allocating an asset's cost over its useful life**. It is not cash paid for a new asset, not a liability owed to the bank, and not a reduction in liabilities.

key_terms.meaning: Spreading the cost of a long-term asset over the years it's used, instead of expensing it all at once.
Annual Depreciation = (Cost - Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life.

chunks.exam_line: Annual Depreciation = (Cost - Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life. Van: ($32,000 - $2,000) ÷ 5 = $6,000 per year.

clarification.text: The amount the business expects to get for the asset at the end of its useful life. That part of the cost is not used up, so it is not spread over the years.

chunks.heading: The five-year depreciation schedule
chunks.explanation_md:
The slide lays out the van's **5-year depreciation schedule**:

| Year | Depreciation expense | Accumulated depreciation | Book value (end of year) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $6,000 | $6,000 | $26,000 |
| 2 | $6,000 | $12,000 | $20,000 |
| 3 | $6,000 | $18,000 | $14,000 |
| 4 | $6,000 | $24,000 | $8,000 |
| 5 | $6,000 | $30,000 | $2,000 |

**How to read it:**
- **Depreciation expense** is the same $6,000 every year. That is what makes it straight-line.
- **Accumulated depreciation** is the running total: it grows by $6,000 a year, reaching $30,000.
- **Book value** is the cost less accumulated depreciation. Year 1: $32,000 - $6,000 = $26,000.
- At the end of year 5 the book value is **$2,000**, exactly the **salvage value**.

**Where depreciation shows up in the statements** (the statement examples use $2,000 of depreciation, not the van): as an expense on the income statement, as accumulated depreciation subtracted from equipment on the balance sheet, and as a non-cash add-back on the cash flow statement.

key_terms.meaning: The running total of depreciation charged so far; $30,000 for the van after 5 years.
Cost less accumulated depreciation; the van's is $2,000 at the end of year 5.

chunks.exam_line: Van book value falls by $6,000 a year: $26,000, $20,000, $14,000, $8,000, and $2,000 (the salvage value) after year 5.

questions.model_answer_md:
The difference is **timing**: when are revenue and expenses recorded?

| Point | Cash Basis | Accrual Basis |

questions.stem: Using the straight-line method, compute the annual depreciation on Northstar's delivery van and its book value at the end of years 2 and 4.
questions.model_answer_md:
Straight-line depreciation spreads the usable cost evenly over the asset's life.

**Formula:** Annual Depreciation = (Cost - Salvage Value) / Useful Life

**Given:** cost $32,000; salvage value $2,000; useful life 5 years.

**Annual depreciation** = (32,000 - 2,000) / 5 = 30,000 / 5 = **$6,000 per year**

**End of year 2:** accumulated depreciation 6,000 x 2 = $12,000; book value 32,000 - 12,000 = **$20,000**

**End of year 4:** accumulated depreciation 6,000 x 4 = $24,000; book value 32,000 - 24,000 = **$8,000**

**Conclusion:** book value falls by $6,000 each year and reaches the $2,000 salvage value at the end of year 5.

rubric.point: Formula (Cost - Salvage) / Useful Life
Year 2: accumulated 12,000, book value 20,000
Year 4: accumulated 24,000, book value 8,000

questions.stem: How do the revenue recognition and matching principles support accrual accounting?
questions.model_answer_md:
Accrual accounting times revenue and expenses to when they occur, and two GAAP principles back this up.

- **Revenue recognition:** recognize revenue when it is **earned**, not necessarily when cash is received. Northstar's $2,000 bike build is revenue of December 2025 even though cash came in January 2026.
- **Matching principle:** match expenses to the revenue they helped generate, **in the same period**. Depreciation applies this by spreading an asset's cost over the years it is used.

**Conclusion:** together they make each period's profit reflect the work done in that period, which is why accrual is required under GAAP for most companies.

rubric.point: Revenue recognised when earned, not when cash received
Matching: expenses in the same period as related revenue
Bike build recorded in December 2025 under accrual
Accrual times revenue and expenses to when they occur

questions.stem: Northstar Bike Co. buys a delivery van for $32,000 with a salvage value of $2,000 and a useful life of 5 years. Explain depreciation, prepare the five-year straight-line schedule, and explain where Northstar's depreciation shows up in its financial statements.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Depreciation** spreads the cost of a long-term asset over the years it is used, instead of expensing it all at once.

**Straight-line formula:** Annual Depreciation = (Cost - Salvage Value) / Useful Life

**Annual charge** = (32,000 - 2,000) / 5 = 30,000 / 5 = **$6,000 per year**

**Five-year schedule**

| Year | Depreciation Expense | Accumulated Depreciation | Book Value (end of year) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6,000 | 6,000 | 32,000 - 6,000 = 26,000 |
| 2 | 6,000 | 12,000 | 20,000 |
| 3 | 6,000 | 18,000 | 14,000 |
| 4 | 6,000 | 24,000 | 8,000 |
| 5 | 6,000 | 30,000 | 2,000 |

**Reading the schedule**
- The expense is the same every year, which is what makes it straight-line.
- Accumulated depreciation builds up by $6,000 a year to $30,000, the cost less salvage value.
- Book value ends at **$2,000, the salvage value**, because that part of the cost is never used up.

**Where depreciation appears (Northstar's 2025 statements)**
- **Income statement:** depreciation of $2,000 is an operating expense.
- **Balance sheet:** accumulated depreciation of $2,000 is deducted from equipment of $14,000, giving $12,000 net.
- **Cash flow statement:** the $2,000 is added back to net income because it is non-cash.

**Conclusion:** straight-line depreciation charges an equal $6,000 a year for the van, and the same idea links all three statements.

rubric.point: Depreciation spreads asset cost over useful life
Ends at salvage value 2,000; accumulated 30,000
Income statement expense; balance sheet accumulated depreciation
Non-cash add-back in cash flow statement

questions.stem: Northstar Bike Co. completes a custom bike build on December 28, 2025 and invoices the client $2,000; the client pays on January 15, 2026. Discuss how this is treated under the cash and accrual bases, which basis GAAP requires, and what it means for reading Northstar's profit and cash.
questions.model_answer_md:
The two bases differ only in **timing**: when revenue and expenses are recorded.

**Cash basis**
- Records revenue **when cash is received** and expenses when cash is paid.
- The $2,000 is revenue of **January 2026**, when the client pays.
- Simple; used by small businesses and freelancers.

**Accrual basis**
- Records revenue **when earned** and expenses **when incurred**, regardless of when cash moves.
- The work was finished in December, so the $2,000 is revenue of **December 2025**.
- It matches revenue to the period it was earned.

**What GAAP says**
- Accrual is **required under GAAP for most companies**.
- It follows the **revenue recognition** principle (recognize revenue when earned, not necessarily when cash is received) and the **matching** principle (expenses in the same period as the revenue they helped generate).

**Reading profit and cash**
- Under accrual, Northstar's 2025 profit includes the $2,000 while the cash only arrives in 2026, so profit and cash differ.
- Sales not yet collected show up as an increase in receivables, which the cash flow statement subtracts from net income.
- This is why a business can show strong net income but low cash on hand, and why the cash flow statement is the one to check first.

**Conclusion:** accrual gives the truer picture of 2025 performance, while the cash flow statement explains the cash that has not yet come in.

rubric.point: Cash basis: $2,000 recorded January 2026 when paid
Accrual: $2,000 recorded December 2025 when earned
Accrual required under GAAP for most companies
Revenue recognition and matching principles
Profit can differ from cash; increase in receivables
Check the cash flow statement first
